title: Using AI to build a welcoming skeleton game: feedback on control clarity and the survival loop?
author: Fickle_Bullfrog_4040
selftext:
I’m developing Hollow Season with First Bloom Games using Codex for AI-assisted implementation and iteration. It’s a free Three.js browser game: a skeleton scares townsfolk to refill a slowly draining life meter, then gets to enjoy pumpkin carving, apple bobbing, and bonfire dancing.

Playable build: https://firstbloomgames.com/games/hollow-season/
Actual game-engine showcase: https://firstbloomgames.com/media/hollow-season/

A concrete lesson from this iteration was that the interaction feedback needed as much attention as the feature list. The game now uses the same targeting function for the mint ring around a nearby NPC and for deciding whether a scare lands. It measures ground distance, so jumping does not unexpectedly reduce your reach. An empty scare only has a short retry delay, while a successful scare keeps the normal cooldown. These are small implementation changes, but they make the next action easier to understand.

Another useful check was the pumpkin and apple stations. The skeleton could trigger an activity while standing too far from the prop; he now steps into position before the animation starts. There are also big on-screen controls, a full-life practice tutorial, and a voluntary feedback card that pauses the run. Browser testing caught details that model-level checks alone did not.

I’d value fresh player feedback, especially from anyone who finds keyboard games awkward. In the first few minutes, is the next action clear? Does the life drain give the autumn activities purpose, or make them feel rushed? If you try it, one confusing moment is as helpful as a long review.

This is an AI-assisted development project, and I’m involved in its direction and iteration. The footage shows the actual engine with staged camera cuts and captions. No download or account needed. Thanks for giving it some of your time.
